entry.title: One update or one per step: how RL and SFT teach a transformer a chain of thought

link.title: One update or one per step: how RL and SFT teach a transformer a chain of thought

entry.content:
27 November 2026 · ICML 2026

One update or one per step: how RL and SFT teach a transformer a chain of thought

Zhanxing Zhu · Joint work with Bochen Lyu, Yiyang Jia and Xiaohao Cai

ICML paperPDFarXivOpenReview

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) both teach language models to write out intermediate steps, a chain of thought, before they answer[1]. Do they teach it in the same way? In our ICML 2026 paper we answer this for a one-layer transformer that learns sparse Boolean functions such as parity. Both methods provably learn the task, but in a different order: RL with a reward for every step learns the whole chain in one update, while SFT on the model’s own steps learns it one step per update. What sets the order is not RL or SFT as such, but whether each step gets feedback that fits the state the model is trained on.

Colour means the same thing in every figure:

inputs, and what is not learned yet the right positions and correct steps positions to ignore, and missing signal RL and its rewards SFT and its labels

Labels followed by a small dot • and terms with a dotted underline carry a note. Hover over them, or tap. In Figs. 6 and 7 the notes sit on the axes and panel captions of the reproduced pictures, and on our labels. Sections 8 to 13, after the story, give the theory in detail.

1. A task that needs intermediate steps

Why does parity need a chain of thought?

We study functions of many bits that depend on only a few of them. Parity is the hardest of these to learn in one go, but it splits into a tree of two-bit steps, as in earlier work on sub-task decomposition[3][4] (Fig. 1).

2. What the transformer has to learn

What must the model get right at each step?

The model is a single attention layer that writes the chain token by token and feeds each token back in. For every token, learning comes down to finding the two positions it should read (Fig. 2).

3. Four ways to give feedback

What feedback does each step of the chain receive?

RL scores the model’s own sampled chains with rewards, and SFT compares them with labels. Within each, one choice decides what a step learns from: rewards for every step or for the answer only, and correct or self-generated previous steps (Fig. 3).

4. One signed update moves attention onto the children

Why can a single update be enough?

Our analysis reduces learnability to one quantity, the critical gradient component. If, in expectation, it is larger at a token’s two children than at any other position, a signed gradient step moves that token’s attention straight towards the children (Fig. 4).

5. All at once, or one step at a time

In which order does each kind of feedback teach the steps?

Given feedback on every step, RL and SFT both meet the separation condition, for parity, AND and OR alike. What differs is how many steps meet it at each update (Fig. 5).

6. RL’s first gradient already points at every child

Does a trained transformer follow the theory under RL?

We trained the transformer on parity of 16 bits out of 20, a chain of four steps, with 50,000 training samples. At initialisation, the sign of the RL policy gradient already matches the target attention in steps 1, 2 and 3, and step 4 has nothing to learn (Fig. 6).

7. SFT’s gradient moves on one step per update

And under SFT on the model’s own steps?

On the same task, the SFT gradient is non-zero for one step at a time, in order: step 1 at the first update, step 2 at the second, step 3 at the third (Fig. 7).

The order does not come from RL or SFT as such. Give SFT correct prefixes and it learns every step at once, like RL with process rewards; give RL rewards whose labels come from the input rather than from its own previous step, and it turns step-wise like SFT (App. H). What matters is whether each step’s feedback is informative for the state the model is trained on, so comparisons such as “SFT memorizes, RL generalizes”[7] should state how supervision and trajectories are coupled. Our analysis is for a one-layer transformer with a structured mask; multi-layer models, realistic reasoning tasks and finite samples come next.

For experts

The seven figures above tell the story. The sections below give the formal version for readers who want it: the exact setting, the quantity that drives learning, the theorems with their conditions, and how the proofs go. Equation, theorem and appendix numbers are those of the paper, so each piece can be looked up.

8. The setting, formally

Which functions, which model, and which target?

The functions. Inputs x are uniform on {−1, +1}d. A k-sparse Boolean function Φk depends only on the bits in a hidden set B ⊆ [d] of size k, with 2 ≤ k ≤ d (Def. 2.1). The paper takes k = 2T and functions that a complete binary tree of one fixed two-bit function ϕ2 computes level by level (Eq. 1):

y(t)j = ϕ2(y(t−1)c1(j), y(t−1)c2(j)),  t = 1, …, T,  j = 1, …, dt = k/2t,  y(0) = x(1)

Step t of the chain has dt tokens, the last token y(T)1 is Φk(x), and c1(j), c2(j), the children of token j, are its relevant positions. Table 1 of the paper pairs each function with an activation ψ:

functionϕ2(z1, z2)ψ(z)
k-PARITYz1z2z2
k-AND(z1z2 + z1 + z2 − 1)/2max(z, 0)
k-OR(−z1z2 + z1 + z2 + 1)/2min(z, 0) + 1

The model. One attention layer reads the sequence z = (x, y), whose k − 1 chain tokens start at 0, with one-hot positional encodings (Eq. 2). Keys and queries are merged into one matrix W that acts on positions only, and the value reads the token itself, so attention chooses positions and the layer returns a weighted average of token values; a feed-forward layer reduced to the fixed activation ψ turns that average into the output. For a token of step t with children c1 and c2, write Wp and σp for its score and its attention on the p-th token of step t − 1 (Eq. 3):

ξ = dt−1∑p=1 σp y(t−1)p,  σp = eWp ∑q eWq,  output ψ(ξ)(3)

Under RL, ψ(ξ) is the probability of writing +1; under SFT, q̂ = 2ψ(ξ) − 1 is a score and the token written is its sign (Eq. 10). Besides the causal mask, a fixed “pretrained” mask lets step t read only step t − 1, and step 1 only x: a structural prior standing in for pretraining. Every token has its own column of scores, initialised at W(0) = 1, so every token starts with attention 1/dt−1 on each position it can see. The best reward and the lowest loss are reached exactly when every token puts ½ on each child and 0 elsewhere; this attention, softmax(W⋆), is the target.

9. Three objectives, one kind of update

What does each method optimise, and how is it updated?

RL with process rewards. The model samples a whole chain y ∼ pW(·|x), and each step is scored against what is correct given the model’s own previous step (Eq. 5):

R(W) = 𝔼x 𝔼y∼pW [ T∑t=1 rt ],  rt = 1k − 1 dt∑j=1 y(t)j ȳ(t)j(5)

Here ȳ(t)j is ϕ2 of the model’s own tokens at the two children of token j. The exact policy gradient credits step t with all rewards from t onwards (Lemma E.1); the analysis uses the per-step form, which credits each step with its own reward, the one that judges it (Eq. 6). Updates keep only the sign of the gradient:

∇WR = 𝔼 [ T∑t=1 ∇W ln pW(y(t) | y(t−1)) rt ],  W(s + 1) = W(s) + η sign(∇WR)(6)

RL with a final reward. Only the answer is scored: rF = y(T) Φk(x), and the objective is RF(W) = 𝔼[rF].

SFT without teacher forcing. The model writes the whole chain itself, ŷ(t)j = sign(q̂(t)j), each token conditioned on its own earlier tokens, and every step is compared with the label ỹ(t) computed from x by the hinge loss ℓ(q̂, a) = max(0, 1 − q̂a) (Eqs. 10 and 11):

L(W) = 𝔼x T∑t=1 Lt,  Lt = 1k − 1 dt∑j=1 ℓ(q̂(t)j, ỹ(t)j),  W(s + 1) = W(s) − η sign(∇WL)(11)

Both methods take signed steps, a special case of Adam[8], from the same start, which makes them directly comparable. With teacher forcing, SFT would instead generate every step from the true previous step ỹ(t−1) (App. B, Q4).

10. The critical gradient component

Which part of the gradient decides what each token learns?

For a token of step t with children c1 and c2, the critical gradient component at position p is (Eq. 7)

γp(y(t−1)) = 2k − 1 ψ′(ξ) ϕ2(y(t−1)c1, y(t−1)c2) y(t−1)p,  p = 1, …, dt−1(7)

It correlates the value at position p with the correct output, weighted by the slope of ψ. The gradient on the token’s scores is a centred, attention-weighted version of it (Lemma E.2):

∂R∂Wp = 𝔼 [ ( γp −  ∑q σq γq ) σp ](19)

Two facts follow. The gradient sums to zero over p, because adding a constant to all scores leaves the softmax unchanged. And while the scores are still equal, as at W(0), every σp is 1/dt−1, so the gradient is larger at p than at p′ exactly when 𝔼[γp − γp′] > 0 (Eqs. 20 and 21). The separation condition asks this for every child p and every other position p′:

RL:  𝔼x, y(:t−1)∼pW [ γp(y(t−1)) − γp′(y(t−1)) ] > 0(8)
SFT:  𝔼x [ γp(ỹ(t−1)) − γp′(ỹ(t−1)) ] > 0(12)

The two conditions differ only in the previous step they are evaluated on: the model’s own samples under RL, the ground truth under SFT. Under separation, symmetry gives the gradient one value at both children and one at all other positions, and the zero sum makes the first positive and the second negative (Fig. 8).

A signed step discards the magnitudes. From W(0) = 1 it moves both children to 1 + η and every other position to 1 − η, which gives (Eqs. 64 and 66)

σc = 12 + (dt−1 − 2) e−2η,  σp′ = 1dt−1 − 2 + 2e2η,  ‖σ − σ⋆‖1 = 1½ + e2η/(dt−1 − 2) ≤ (dt−1 − 2) e−2η

One update with η ≥ ½ ln(d/ε) therefore brings every token whose gradient has this sign pattern within ε of its target. This is where the η = Ω(ln(d/ε)) of the theorems comes from.

11. RL: the whole chain in one update

What do the RL results guarantee, and where do they stop?

Theorem 3.1 (RL with process rewards)Let d ≥ k ≥ 2, W(0) = 1 and η = Ω(ln(d/ε)) for ε > 0. If the separation condition (8) holds for every step t, every token of it, every child p and every other position p′, then one signed policy-gradient update W(1) = W(0) + η sign(∇WR) gives ‖softmax(W(1)) − softmax(W⋆)‖1 ≤ ε.

Proof idea. Each token has its own column of scores, and the process reward for step t depends only on step t and the model’s own step t − 1. Condition (8) is thus a statement about W(0) for every step at once, however wrong the earlier steps still are. Where it holds, every token’s gradient has the sign pattern of Fig. 8, and the signed step of Section 10 moves all columns in the same update (App. E.3).

For parity the condition can be checked in closed form. At W(0), the gradient gap between a child and any other position is proportional to (1 − c2)((dt−1 − 3)c2 + 1)/d2t−1, which is positive because the tokens of step t − 1 share a mean c with |c| < 1 (Eq. 99, Lemma G.1). The separation persists at every iteration, so after s signed updates (Theorem 4.1)

σc(s) = 12 + (dt−1 − 2) e−2ηs,  σp′(s) = 1dt−1 − 2 + 2e2ηsThm. 4.1

A large step or many small ones reach the target; Fig. 4 plots s = 1. AND and OR satisfy condition (8) as well, with their ψ from Table 1 (Claim 4.2).

Proposition 3.2 (a final reward is hard for parity)Let ℋ be a set of functions h: {−1, +1}d → {−1, +1} with 𝔼x[h(x)h′(x)] = 0 for any two distinct h, h′, and let the model satisfy 𝔼x‖∇W 𝔼y∼pW[y(T)]‖2 ≤ M. With the final reward rFh = y(T)h(x), the policy gradient barely depends on which h is the target:
𝔼h∈ℋ ‖∇WRFh − 𝔼h′∈ℋ ∇WRFh′‖2 ≤ M|ℋ|(9)

All parities on d bits form such a set, with |ℋ| = 2d: for a target drawn from it, the part of the gradient that depends on the target is exponentially small in d, the classic argument against learning parity end to end[2]. This is a hardness result for this reward, not a learning schedule.

12. SFT: one step per update

Why can SFT not learn step t before step t − 1?

Theorem 3.3 (SFT without teacher forcing)Let d ≥ k ≥ 2, W(0) = 1 and η = Ω(ln(d/ε)). If the separation condition (12) holds for every step t, every token of it, every child p and every other position p′, then T signed gradient steps on the loss (11) give ‖softmax(W(T)) − softmax(W⋆)‖1 ≤ ε.

The SFT gradient for step t couples a token’s fixed label with what the model itself wrote at step t − 1. While the token’s scores are equal, the descent direction at p exceeds that at p′ by (1/dt−1)[γp(ŷ(t−1)) − γp′(ŷ(t−1))], where γ is built from the written tokens ŷ(t−1) and the label ỹ(t) (Lemma F.1, Eq. 54). The gap has the sign pattern of Fig. 8 when (i) the token’s scores are still equal, (ii) step t − 1 is written correctly, ŷ(t−1) = ỹ(t−1), and (iii) condition (12) holds (Lemma F.2).

Condition (ii) is the one that fails at first (Fig. 9). At W(0) every token of step 1 averages the same inputs with the same weights, so all of them write the same value (Eq. 75). A token of step 2 then sees one value at all its positions, γp does not depend on p, and its gradient is exactly zero for every input; the same holds for every later step. The sign of zero is zero, so these scores stay equal and condition (i) still holds when their turn comes. Step 1 reads x, which is always correct, so update 1 teaches step 1. From then on step 1 writes ỹ(1), condition (ii) holds for step 2 and update 2 teaches it, and so on up to step T (App. F.1). A step that has been learned keeps only a gradient of order δ = ½ − σc, which the analysis neglects (Eq. 74).

Three variants locate the cause. With teacher forcing, every step reads the true previous step from the start, so condition (ii) holds for all steps at the first update and SFT learns the whole chain at once (App. B, Q4). RL whose step rewards use labels computed from x, rather than from the model’s own previous step, learns step by step; App. H solves these dynamics exactly for chains of one and two steps, which rules out sampled versus deterministic generation as the cause. And a logistic or exponential loss in place of the hinge loss keeps the step-wise schedule (App. F.2). Condition (12) holds for parity (Claim 4.1) and for AND and OR (Claim 4.2).

13. What the assumptions buy

Which assumptions carry the results, and how far do they reach?

The model is deliberately minimal (App. B, Q7): one layer and one head; keys and queries merged into a matrix that acts on positions only; a value that reads the token; a feed-forward layer reduced to an activation matched to the target (Table 1); and the “pretrained” mask, under which each step reads only the previous one. The gradients are population gradients, the updates are signed and start from equal scores, and the conditions are sufficient rather than necessary. Learning should fail where separation fails, as it does with a final reward for parity.

The tree is not essential (App. I). For a serial chain y1 = ϕ2(xi1, xi2), yj = ϕ2(yj−1, xij+1), with a mask that lets token j read all of x and the previous token, the same separation argument holds: RL with process rewards and SFT with teacher forcing learn the whole chain in one update. SFT without teacher forcing then needs a filter that holds back the loss of later tokens until the earlier ones are learned; without it, later tokens get noisy gradients and learning is hard (App. I.2).

Multi-layer and multi-head models, realistic reasoning tasks, finite samples, noisy optimisation and imperfect rewards are left open (App. A).

References

  1. Wei et al. Chain of Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models. NeurIPS 2022.
  2. Shalev-Shwartz et al. Failures of Gradient-Based Deep Learning. 2017.
  3. Wies et al. Sub-Task Decomposition Enables Learning in Sequence to Sequence Tasks. 2023.
  4. Kim and Suzuki. Transformers Provably Solve Parity Efficiently with Chain of Thought. ICLR 2025.
  5. Shao et al. DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models. 2024.
  6. Lightman et al. Let’s Verify Step by Step. ICLR 2024.
  7. Chu et al. SFT Memorizes, RL Generalizes: A Comparative Study of Foundation Model Post-training. ICML 2025.
  8. Kingma and Ba. Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization. 2017.

Figures 1–5, 8 and 9 are our own drawings: Figs. 1, 2 and 9 use an invented 12-bit example, Fig. 3 is a schematic after Fig. 1 of the paper, Figs. 4 and 8 plot values computed from Theorem 4.1 and Lemma E.2, and Fig. 5 summarises Theorems 3.1 and 3.3, Proposition 3.2 and App. B. Figures 6 and 7 reproduce Figures 5 and 6 of the paper unchanged (arXiv version under CC BY 4.0), with guides drawn on top. Sections 8 to 13 follow the paper’s notation in a lighter form, writing σp and Wp for one token’s attention and score on position p.
entry.summary: Why RL with process rewards learns a whole chain of thought in one update while SFT on its own steps learns it one step per update, with the theorems and proofs of our ICML 2026 paper for experts.

entry.title: Learning dynamics on a graph: how STGCN forecasts many coupled time series at once

link.title: Learning dynamics on a graph: how STGCN forecasts many coupled time series at once

entry.content:
26 November 2026

Learning dynamics on a graph: how STGCN forecasts many coupled time series at once

Zhanxing Zhu · Joint work with Bing Yu and Haoteng Yin (IJCAI 2018)

arXivPDFIJCAI proceedingsCodePyTorch port

Many real signals are measured at points that are linked to each other: sensors on roads, stations in a city, electrodes on a scalp. The right object is then a graph whose every node carries a time series. In our IJCAI 2018 paper, we introduced the Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (STGCN) for forecasting these coupled time series. To our knowledge, it was the first model for this problem built entirely from convolutions over the graph and over time. We tested it on road sensors. Its sandwich block became a standard building block of graph neural networks for time series[7], and the paper is among the most cited in that field.

The figures below build the idea one piece at a time. Colour means the same thing in all of them:

space: the graph, its sensors and edges, the graph convolution time: the time axis, past frames, the temporal gated convolution STGCN itself and what it predicts the field that grew from it earlier methods, baselines, and what is unknown

Labels followed by a small dot • and terms with a dotted underline carry a note. Hover over them, or tap. Bars and nodes without a dot carry notes as well.

1. A network of time series

What is forecast, and why draw it as a graph?

Each sensor reports a speed every five minutes, and nearby sensors move together. We treat the readings at one moment as a signal on a graph. Stacking these signals in time lets us forecast the next few frames (Fig. 1).

2. Where earlier models fall short

What do per-series models, grid CNNs and RNNs miss?

Before this paper, forecasters either ignored the network, forced it onto a grid, or read time with recurrent chains. STGCN keeps the graph as it is and reads time with convolutions instead, building on spectral graph convolution[1][2] and convolutional sequence models[3] (Fig. 2).

3. Convolution over the graph

How does a sensor read its neighbours?

A graph has no left and right, so we define our filter through the graph Laplacian and approximate it with polynomials, after Defferrard et al.[1] and Kipf and Welling[2]. In practice a node mixes its own value with those of nodes a few edges away (Fig. 3).

4. Convolution over time, with a gate

How is the time axis read without recurrence?

Along the time axis, we use a plain one-dimensional convolution with a gate, the gated linear unit of Gehring et al.[3]. Every output depends only on a short window of the past, so all positions are computed at once (Fig. 4).

5. The sandwich block and the full network

How do the two convolutions fit together?

The ST-Conv block puts one graph convolution between two temporal ones, and the model stacks two such blocks before an output layer. Each temporal layer shortens the stack of frames by two, so twelve frames come out as one forecast (Fig. 5).

6. Accuracy on 228 and 1,026 sensors

Does it beat the methods it replaces, at every horizon?

On the California highway data (PeMSD7), both STGCN variants have the lowest error at all three horizons, and the gap grows with the horizon (Fig. 6).

7. Training cost

What does the convolutional design buy in time and size?

Because no step waits for the one before, training runs in parallel. We measured the full training time against GCGRU on both PeMSD7 graphs (Fig. 7).

8. Eight years of citations

How widely has the idea been taken up?

Citations of the paper have grown every year since it appeared, and the official code is still maintained. The counts differ between databases, so the figure shows them side by side (Fig. 8).

9. The family it started

What grew from the sandwich block, and where did it travel?

Later models kept the pairing of graph convolution and temporal convolution and changed one part at a time: a learned graph[5], attention, continuous time. The decisive step for the general case was MTGNN[6], which learns the graph from the series themselves, so no map is needed (Fig. 9).

In the paper, we reported that STGCN outperformed the state of the art on two real-world data sets while achieving “faster training, easier convergences, and fewer parameters”, and that the framework “can be applied into more general spatio-temporal structured sequence forecasting scenarios, such as evolving of social networks, and preference prediction in recommendation systems”. The field did exactly that, and the block now reads air-quality stations, EEG electrodes and dengue counts that never stood beside a road[9].

References

  1. Defferrard et al. Convolutional neural networks on graphs with fast localized spectral filtering. NIPS 2016.
  2. Kipf and Welling. Semi-supervised classification with graph convolutional networks. 2016.
  3. Gehring et al. Convolutional sequence to sequence learning. 2017.
  4. Li et al. Diffusion convolutional recurrent neural network: Data-driven traffic forecasting. ICLR 2018.
  5. Wu et al. Graph WaveNet for deep spatial-temporal graph modeling. IJCAI 2019.
  6. Wu et al. Connecting the dots: Multivariate time series forecasting with graph neural networks. KDD 2020.
  7. Jin et al. A survey on graph neural networks for time series: Forecasting, classification, imputation, and anomaly detection. TPAMI 2024.
  8. Corradini et al. A systematic literature review of spatio-temporal graph neural network models for time series forecasting and classification. Neural Networks 2025.
  9. Siabi et al. Innovative application of a traffic-prediction spatio-temporal graph convolutional network for dengue disease forecasting. Scientific Reports 2026.
  10. Lone et al. Efficient traffic prediction at scale: A systematic study of STGCN architectural depth. 2026.

Bing Yu, Haoteng Yin and I presented “Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks: A Deep Learning Framework for Traffic Forecasting” at IJCAI 2018. Figures 1–5 use an illustrative road map and invented readings to explain the method. Figures 6 and 7 plot results from Tables 2 and 3 of our paper. Figure 8 uses citation databases and GitHub, and Figure 9 draws on the follow-up studies named in the timeline.
entry.summary: How our IJCAI 2018 paper used graph and temporal convolutions for multivariate time series forecasting, and how the idea developed over the next eight years.

entry.title: a post with jupyter notebook
entry.content:
To include a jupyter notebook in a post, you can use the following code:

{::nomarkdown} {% assign jupyter_path = "assets/jupyter/blog.ipynb" | relative_url %} {% capture notebook_exists %}{% file_exists
assets/jupyter/blog.ipynb %}{% endcapture %} {% if notebook_exists == "true" %} {% jupyter_notebook jupyter_path %} {% else %}
<p>Sorry, the notebook you are looking for does not exist.</p>
{% endif %} {:/nomarkdown}

Let’s break it down: this is possible thanks to Jekyll Jupyter Notebook plugin that allows you to embed jupyter notebooks in your posts. It basically calls jupyter nbconvert --to html to convert the notebook to an html page and then includes it in the post. Since Kramdown is the default Markdown renderer for Jekyll, we need to surround the call to the plugin with the ::nomarkdown tag so that it stops processing this part with Kramdown and outputs the content as-is.

The plugin takes as input the path to the notebook, but it assumes the file exists. If you want to check if the file exists before calling the plugin, you can use the file_exists filter. This avoids getting a 404 error from the plugin and ending up displaying the main page inside of it instead. If the file does not exist, you can output a message to the user. The code displayed above outputs the following:

Note that the jupyter notebook supports both light and dark themes.

entry.title: a post with custom blockquotes
entry.content:
This post shows how to add custom styles for blockquotes. Based on jekyll-gitbook implementation.

We decided to support the same custom blockquotes as in jekyll-gitbook, which are also found in a lot of other sites’ styles. The styles definitions can be found on the _base.scss file, more specifically:

/* Tips, warnings, and dangers */
.post .post-content blockquote {
  &.block-tip {
    border-color: var(--global-tip-block);
    background-color: var(--global-tip-block-bg);

    p {
      color: var(--global-tip-block-text);
    }

    h1,
    h2,
    h3,
    h4,
    h5,
    h6 {
      color: var(--global-tip-block-title);
    }
  }

  &.block-warning {
    border-color: var(--global-warning-block);
    background-color: var(--global-warning-block-bg);

    p {
      color: var(--global-warning-block-text);
    }

    h1,
    h2,
    h3,
    h4,
    h5,
    h6 {
      color: var(--global-warning-block-title);
    }
  }

  &.block-danger {
    border-color: var(--global-danger-block);
    background-color: var(--global-danger-block-bg);

    p {
      color: var(--global-danger-block-text);
    }

    h1,
    h2,
    h3,
    h4,
    h5,
    h6 {
      color: var(--global-danger-block-title);
    }
  }
}

A regular blockquote can be used as following:

> This is a regular blockquote
> and it can be used as usual

This is a regular blockquote and it can be used as usual

These custom styles can be used by adding the specific class to the blockquote, as follows:

> ##### TIP
>
> A tip can be used when you want to give advice
> related to a certain content.
> {: .block-tip }
TIP

A tip can be used when you want to give advice related to a certain content.

> ##### WARNING
>
> This is a warning, and thus should
> be used when you want to warn the user
> {: .block-warning }
WARNING

This is a warning, and thus should be used when you want to warn the user

> ##### DANGER
>
> This is a danger zone, and thus should
> be used carefully

link.title: a post with table of contents on a sidebar

entry.content:
This post shows how to add a table of contents as a sidebar.

Adding a Table of Contents

To add a table of contents to a post as a sidebar, simply add

toc:
  sidebar: left

to the front matter of the post. The table of contents will be automatically generated from the headings in the post. If you wish to display the sidebar to the right, simply change left to right.

entry.title: displaying beautiful tables with Bootstrap Tables

link.title: displaying beautiful tables with Bootstrap Tables

entry.content:
Using markdown to display tables is easy. Just use the following syntax:

| Left aligned | Center aligned | Right aligned |
| :----------- | :------------: | ------------: |
| Left 1       |    center 1    |       right 1 |
| Left 2       |    center 2    |       right 2 |
| Left 3       |    center 3    |       right 3 |

That will generate:

Left aligned Center aligned Right aligned
Left 1 center 1 right 1
Left 2 center 2 right 2
Left 3 center 3 right 3

It is also possible to use HTML to display tables. For example, the following HTML code will display a table with Bootstrap Table, loaded from a JSON file:

<table id="table" data-toggle="table" data-url="{{ '/assets/json/table_data.json' | relative_url }}">
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th data-field="id">ID</th>
      <th data-field="name">Item Name</th>
      <th data-field="price">Item Price</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
</table>
ID Item Name Item Price

By using Bootstrap Table it is possible to create pretty complex tables, with pagination, search, and more. For example, the following HTML code will display a table, loaded from a JSON file, with pagination, search, checkboxes, and header/content alignment. For more information, check the documentation.

<table
  data-click-to-select="true"
  data-height="460"
  data-pagination="true"
  data-search="true"
  data-toggle="table"
  data-url="{{ '/assets/json/table_data.json' | relative_url }}"
>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th data-checkbox="true"></th>
      <th data-field="id" data-halign="left" data-align="center" data-sortable="true">ID</th>
      <th data-field="name" data-halign="center" data-align="right" data-sortable="true">Item Name</th>
      <th data-field="price" data-halign="right" data-align="left" data-sortable="true">Item Price</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
</table>
ID Item Name Item Price
